client: Lately, I’ve been feeling completely drained by my new job at the tech startup. I’ve been pulling late hours almost every night for the past month, and it’s starting to feel like I can’t keep up. I’m not sure therapy can help with this—it’s just the nature of the job, right? But I’m so overwhelmed, and I don’t know how to handle it.
therapist:
It sounds like you're feeling both physically exhausted and emotionally overwhelmed by the demands of this new job. I notice you seem to have mixed feelings—acknowledging how hard it is while also questioning whether it's something that can or should change. 

What thoughts come up for you when you imagine setting some boundaries around your work hours?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: I worry that if I try to set boundaries, they'll think I'm not committed enough. Everyone else seems to be working just as late, and I don't want to be the weak link. But at the same time, I'm barely functioning—I snapped at my partner last night over nothing.
therapist:
You're caught between two understandable but painful fears—being seen as inadequate at work, and burning out to the point where it affects your personal life. I hear how urgent this feels in your voice—that tension between keeping up and breaking down. 

What do you think would happen if you experimented with one small boundary, just for a week, to test whether your worry about being seen as "weak" actually comes true?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: I guess I could try leaving by 7pm instead of 9pm for a few days... but honestly, just thinking about it makes me anxious. What if there's an emergency and I'm not there? Or what if my manager notices and thinks I'm slacking when everyone else is staying late?
therapist:
I hear that anxiety bubbling up just at the thought of trying this small change—your voice gets quicker and higher when you imagine those "what if" scenarios. That tells me this experiment feels risky to you in ways that go beyond just work hours. 

What's the worst-case scenario your mind is picturing that makes this feel so dangerous to try?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client:
I keep imagining getting called into HR and being told I'm not "startup material." That phrase actually keeps me up at night. My last performance review was great, but I can't shake this fear that one small change will make them see me differently. 

It feels like I'm walking on a tightrope where any shift in balance could ruin everything I've worked for.
therapist:
It sounds like this fear of being labeled "not startup material" carries a lot of weight for you—it's clearly more than just about work hours. I notice your voice softens when you mention your good performance review, almost like part of you knows this fear might be bigger than the facts.

What does being "startup material" mean to you personally, and how much of that definition feels like something you genuinely identify with versus something you feel pressured to live up to?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client:
That's... actually really hard to answer. I used to think being "startup material" meant being passionate and innovative, but lately it just feels like code for "works themselves to death." I see the way people brag about pulling all-nighters like it's a badge of honor, and part of me wants that recognition too—but another part just feels exhausted by the whole culture. 

It's confusing because I do love the actual work, just not this unsustainable pace.
therapist:
There's real pain in your voice as you describe this tension—loving the work but feeling worn down by the expectations around it. That word "unsustainable" stood out—it sounds like your body and mind are sending strong signals about what this pace is costing you. 

When you notice that pull between wanting recognition and feeling exhausted by the culture, where does that leave your sense of what truly matters to you in your career?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, loud, fast speech

client: I think what truly matters to me is doing meaningful work and growing my skills—not just racking up hours to prove I’m dedicated. But it’s hard to hold onto that when everyone around me seems to value the grind itself over the actual results. I’m scared that if I prioritize balance, I’ll lose respect or opportunities, even if it’s better for me in the long run.
therapist:
I hear how clearly you've identified what matters most to you—the work itself and your growth—but how scary it feels to honor that when the culture seems to reward something different. Your voice speeds up when you talk about losing respect, like this fear has real momentum behind it.  

What would it look like to test whether the people whose opinions matter most to you—maybe your manager or a respected colleague—actually share those "grind-over-results" values as much as you fear they do?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, very rapid speech

client:
I could try asking my manager directly about expectations, but the thought of that conversation makes my stomach drop. What if confirming they do value long hours forces me to either sacrifice my health or quit? 

Part of me worries this test would just prove what I'm afraid of—that results only matter when they come with suffering.
therapist:
You're describing this potential conversation with your manager with such visceral dread—your voice gets very quiet, like you're bracing for a blow. That tells me this isn't just about gathering information, but about how exposed this question might make you feel. 

When you imagine having this talk, which feels scarier: discovering their expectations are unreasonable, or realizing you might need to make a difficult choice about staying in this environment?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, very quiet, moderate-paced speech

client:
Honestly, both options terrify me in different ways. If their expectations are unreasonable, I'd have to confront how toxic this culture really is. But if I realize I need to leave, that means starting over somewhere else after investing so much here. 

I think what scares me most is either way, it would mean admitting to myself that this isn't working—and I'm not sure I'm ready to face that yet.
therapist:
I hear how much weight this realization carries for you—that facing either possibility would mean acknowledging a painful truth about this situation. Your voice sounds heavier as you talk about not being ready to face this, like it's something you've been trying to avoid looking at directly. 

What would it feel like to give yourself permission to simply notice these feelings without having to act on them right away?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client:
That’s... actually a relief to hear. I’ve been putting so much pressure on myself to figure this out immediately, like I need to have all the answers right now. But just letting myself notice how I feel without rushing to fix it—that feels like it could take some of the weight off. 

Still, part of me worries that if I don’t act soon, things will just keep getting worse. It’s hard to trust that it’s okay to take time with this.
therapist:
It's beautiful to hear that relief in your voice when you consider taking some pressure off yourself—that fast, brighter tone tells me this idea genuinely resonates with you. Yet I also hear that persistent worry underneath, that old habit of urgency creeping back in.  

What would it look like to balance both—honoring this new sense of permission while also setting a gentle timeline to check in with yourself about next steps?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client:
Maybe I could give myself two weeks just to observe - notice how I feel when I leave earlier some days, pay attention to any actual consequences, not just the fears. But what if nothing changes in those two weeks? 

I like the idea of a timeline, but part of me still panics thinking that in two weeks I might be in exactly the same stuck place, just two weeks more exhausted.
therapist:
I hear how hopeful you sound about giving yourself this observation period, but also how quickly that hope gets tangled up with worries about whether it will actually help. Your voice rises with that panic about being stuck—it’s clear this feels like such a delicate balance.  

What would it mean to view these two weeks not as a test to fix everything, but as a chance to gather information about what’s working and what’s not, even if the changes are small?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech
